questions.stem: Antisocial behaviour is best described as behaviour that:
options: is intended to benefit another person without any reward
follows the direct instructions of a legitimate authority figure
matches the norms of a group so that a person is accepted
harms others or disregards their wellbeing and the rules of society
questions.explanation: Antisocial behaviour harms or disrupts others, or ignores their wellbeing and social rules. Behaviour intended to benefit others is prosocial.

questions.stem: Prosocial behaviour is best described as:
options: behaviour that harms others to gain an advantage
behaviour that copies a group to avoid rejection
voluntary behaviour intended to benefit other people
behaviour that follows the rules only when watched
questions.explanation: Prosocial behaviour is any voluntary action intended to help or benefit others, such as sharing, comforting or helping. Following rules only when watched is compliance.

questions.stem: The bystander effect is the finding that:
options: people in a good mood are less likely to help others
people are less likely to help in an emergency when others are present
people are more likely to help in an emergency when others are present
people help only those who have helped them in the past
questions.explanation: The bystander effect is the tendency for any one person to be less likely to help in an emergency when other people are present. Helping those who have helped us is the reciprocity principle.

questions.stem: Diffusion of responsibility is:
options: weighing up the costs of helping against the costs of not helping
each person feeling less responsible to act because others are present
the fear of being embarrassed in front of others if one acts wrongly
using other people's reactions to decide whether a situation is really serious
questions.explanation: When several people witness an emergency, responsibility is spread among them, so each person feels less obliged to act. Fear of embarrassment is audience inhibition.

questions.stem: A man collapses on a crowded train platform. Many people see him, but each assumes someone else will call for help, so nobody does. Which factor best explains this?
options: Groupthink
Diffusion of responsibility
Audience inhibition
The reciprocity principle
questions.explanation: Each bystander assumes someone else will act, so responsibility is spread thinly and nobody acts, which is diffusion of responsibility. Audience inhibition involves fear of looking foolish.

questions.stem: Audience inhibition is:
options: feeling less responsible to help because many others are present
losing one's sense of identity when part of a large anonymous group
helping someone because they have helped you in the past
holding back from helping for fear of being embarrassed or judged
questions.explanation: Audience inhibition is holding back from helping because of a fear of looking foolish if the situation turns out not to be an emergency, or of being judged for helping badly. Feeling less responsible because others are present is diffusion of responsibility.

questions.stem: Ayla hears shouting from a park and wonders whether someone is in trouble, but she does nothing because she would feel silly if it were just friends mucking around. Which factor best explains her behaviour?
options: Diffusion of responsibility
Social responsibility
Reciprocity
Audience inhibition
questions.explanation: Ayla holds back because she fears embarrassment if she has misjudged the situation, which is audience inhibition. Diffusion of responsibility would involve assuming someone else will deal with it.

questions.stem: In an ambiguous situation, bystanders look at each other, see that nobody seems worried, and conclude that nothing is wrong. Which factor does this show?
options: Altruism
Reciprocity
Social influence
Cost-benefit analysis
questions.explanation: Bystanders use each other's reactions to interpret an unclear situation, and if others appear calm they conclude it is not an emergency. This is social influence, and it can stop anyone from helping.

questions.stem: In the context of helping, a cost-benefit analysis involves:
options: helping only people who have already helped you in the past
copying what most other bystanders are doing at the time
weighing the costs of helping against the costs of not helping
comparing one's own group with other groups to raise self-esteem
questions.explanation: A person weighs up costs of helping, such as danger, time and effort, against costs of not helping, such as guilt or blame. When helping seems too costly, people are less likely to help.

questions.stem: Running late for an important exam, Liam passes a stranger struggling to change a flat tyre and keeps walking, although he would usually stop. Which factor best explains his choice?
options: Cost-benefit analysis
Diffusion of responsibility
Audience inhibition
Groupthink
questions.explanation: For Liam, the cost of helping, missing his exam, outweighs the cost of not helping, so he keeps going. There are no other bystanders, so diffusion of responsibility does not apply.

questions.stem: What was the aim of Latane and Darley's 1968 smoke-filled room study?
options: To find out whether competition between groups causes prejudice and hostility
To find out whether the presence of others affects whether people report an emergency
To find out whether people obey an authority figure who orders them to harm someone
To find out whether people conform to a group that gives obviously wrong answers
questions.explanation: Latane and Darley investigated whether people are less likely to respond to a possible emergency, smoke entering a room, when others are present. Obedience was the focus of Milgram's study.

questions.stem: In Latane and Darley's study, what was happening when smoke began to pour into the room?
options: Participants were filling in a questionnaire, either alone or with others
Participants were giving electric shocks to a learner in the next room
Participants were judging the length of lines with a group of confederates
Participants were watching a film about emergencies with friends
questions.explanation: Male university students were filling in a questionnaire when smoke began to come through a wall vent. They were alone, with two passive confederates, or with two other real participants.

questions.stem: Which result did Latane and Darley find?
options: Every participant reported the smoke within a minute, whether alone or with others
Participants reported the smoke more often when the others in the room ignored it
About three-quarters of participants alone reported the smoke, but only 1 in 10 with two passive confederates did
About three-quarters of participants with two passive confederates reported the smoke, but only 1 in 10 alone did
questions.explanation: About 75% of participants alone reported the smoke, compared with only 10% of those sitting with two confederates who ignored it. The presence of passive others strongly inhibited responding.

questions.stem: Why did so few participants report the smoke when sitting with two passive confederates?
options: They could not see the smoke because the confederates blocked the vent
They were paid extra money for finishing the questionnaire
They used the confederates' calm as a sign the smoke was not dangerous
They were directly ordered by the confederates not to leave the room
questions.explanation: Seeing others ignore the smoke led participants to interpret the situation as harmless, a form of social influence, and fear of overreacting in front of others also played a part. Nobody ordered them to stay.

questions.stem: In groups of three real participants, someone reported the smoke in far fewer groups than would be expected if each person behaved as they did alone. What does this suggest?
options: Participants in groups noticed the smoke later because they were talking to each other
The questionnaire was harder in groups, so participants concentrated more on it
Three people are too many for anyone to notice smoke entering a room
Participants were inhibited by each other's inaction, even though none were confederates
questions.explanation: Each real participant hesitated, saw others hesitating and took that as a sign nothing was wrong, so inaction spread through the group. This showed the bystander effect without any confederates.

questions.stem: Which is a valid criticism of Latane and Darley's smoke-filled room study?
options: The study had no comparison condition in which participants sat on their own
The participants were told the smoke was part of the study beforehand
The study took place in a busy street, so conditions could not be controlled
The participants were all male university students, which limits generalisability
questions.explanation: A sample of male university students limits how far the findings can be applied to others. The study did have an alone condition, and participants were not told in advance about the smoke.

questions.stem: Which ethical concern applies to the smoke-filled room study?
options: Participants were kept in the room for several days without a break
Participants were deceived and may have felt real fear that there was a fire
Participants were given electric shocks whenever they failed to report the smoke
Participants were children who could not legally give their own consent
questions.explanation: Participants did not know the smoke was staged, so they were deceived and may have experienced anxiety. No shocks were involved, and the participants were adult students.

questions.stem: What was the main contribution of the smoke-filled room study?
options: It showed that people respond fastest to emergencies when they are in large groups
It showed that only people with uncaring personalities ignore emergencies
It showed that people always obey instructions from the person in charge
It showed others' presence can stop people responding to a possible emergency
questions.explanation: The study showed that situational factors, especially the reactions of others, can stop people from acting in an emergency, supporting the idea of the bystander effect. It suggested the situation, not personality, explains non-intervention.

questions.stem: Groupthink is:
options: a close-knit group valuing agreement over careful, critical decision-making
the tendency of a group to make better decisions than any individual member could make alone
the tendency of group members to feel less responsible to act in an emergency
a belief that the world is fair, so people end up getting what they deserve
questions.explanation: Groupthink occurs when the desire for harmony and agreement in a cohesive group overrides realistic evaluation of options, leading to poor decisions. Feeling less responsible in an emergency is diffusion of responsibility.

questions.stem: A tight-knit committee approves a risky plan. Several members have doubts but keep quiet, assuming everyone else agrees. Which symptom of groupthink is shown?
options: A superordinate goal shared by all members
Self-censorship and an illusion of unanimity
Diffusion of responsibility in an emergency
Audience inhibition caused by fear of embarrassment
questions.explanation: Members holding back their doubts is self-censorship, and their belief that everyone agrees is an illusion of unanimity. Both are classic symptoms of groupthink.

questions.stem: Which step would best reduce the risk of groupthink in a decision-making group?
options: Having the leader announce the preferred option at the very start
Making sure all members come from the same background
Discouraging members from seeking advice from outsiders
Appointing a member to argue against the group's preferred option
questions.explanation: Having someone play devil's advocate encourages critical evaluation of options and makes it easier to voice doubts. A leader stating a preference early, a uniform group and isolation from outsiders all make groupthink more likely.

questions.stem: A group of friends agrees to a cruel prank on a classmate. Each privately thinks it is wrong, but nobody says so because the group seems so united. How does this illustrate antisocial behaviour arising from social influence?
options: Informational influence led the group to look up the correct answer
Groupthink led the group to an antisocial decision that no member would have made alone
Altruism led each member to put the classmate's welfare ahead of their own
The reciprocity principle led the group to repay the classmate for an earlier favour
questions.explanation: Pressure to stay united stopped members voicing doubts, so the group chose a harmful action, an example of groupthink producing antisocial behaviour. Altruism and reciprocity are factors that increase prosocial behaviour.

questions.stem: Which description best defines bullying?
options: Repeated, deliberate behaviour that misuses power to cause harm
A single heated argument between two friends of equal standing
Any disagreement in which one of the people involved loses their temper
Friendly teasing that both people find funny
questions.explanation: Bullying is ongoing and deliberate, involves an imbalance of power, and is intended to cause physical, social or psychological harm. A one-off argument between equals is conflict, not bullying.

questions.stem: A student repeatedly spreads rumours about a classmate and persuades others to leave her out. Which type of bullying is this?
options: Social bullying
Physical bullying
Verbal bullying
Cyberbullying
questions.explanation: Deliberately damaging someone's relationships or reputation, through rumours and exclusion, is social (relational) bullying. Physical bullying involves hurting a person's body or property.

questions.stem: Which situation is an example of bullying rather than ordinary conflict?
options: Two friends argue once about whose turn it is to choose a game
Two teammates disagree about tactics at training and then sort it out
A student is upset after losing a fair debate in class
An older student targets a younger one with insults every day for weeks
questions.explanation: Bullying is repeated, deliberate and involves a power imbalance, as when an older student targets a younger one every day. A single disagreement between equals is conflict.

questions.stem: Theo starts mocking a classmate online because the popular group in his year is doing it. Which explanation best accounts for his behaviour?
options: Social influence, as he conforms to the group's behaviour to fit in
Altruism, as he expects nothing in return for his behaviour
Diffusion of responsibility, as he waits for others to help the victim
Competence, as he has the skills needed to help in the situation
questions.explanation: Theo joins in because the group he wants to belong to is doing it, so social influence (normative conformity) leads to antisocial behaviour. Diffusion of responsibility explains failing to help, not joining in.

questions.stem: The reciprocity principle states that people:
options: help more when they have relevant skills
tend to help those who have helped them
should help those who depend on them
help more when they are in a good mood
questions.explanation: The reciprocity principle is the expectation that we should return help to those who have helped us. Helping those who depend on us is the social responsibility norm.

questions.stem: The social responsibility norm is the belief that people should:
options: help only members of their own group
help those who need or depend on them, expecting nothing back
help only those who have helped them in the past
help only when the benefits clearly outweigh the costs to themselves
questions.explanation: The social responsibility norm is the expectation that we should help those who are dependent on us or in need, such as children, older people or people with a disability, regardless of any return.

questions.stem: Last month Huy's neighbour helped him move house. When the neighbour asks for help with a fence, Huy agrees straight away. Which factor best explains this?
options: Diffusion of responsibility
The reciprocity principle
The social responsibility norm
Audience inhibition
questions.explanation: Huy returns the help his neighbour gave him, which is the reciprocity principle. The social responsibility norm applies to helping those in need regardless of past favours.

questions.stem: Ruby sees an elderly stranger drop her shopping in the car park and stops to help pick it up. Which factor best explains this?
options: Groupthink
The social responsibility norm
The reciprocity principle
Deindividuation
questions.explanation: Ruby helps a person in need who has done nothing for her, consistent with the social responsibility norm. The reciprocity principle would require the stranger to have helped Ruby first.

questions.stem: Which personal characteristic involves understanding and sharing another person's feelings, and makes helping more likely?
options: Conformity
Empathy
Competence
Reciprocity
questions.explanation: Empathy is the ability to understand and share another person's feelings, and people who feel empathy for someone in need are more likely to help. Competence is having the skills needed to help.

questions.stem: Research has found that people who have just had a pleasant experience, such as finding money, are more likely to help a stranger. Which personal characteristic does this show?
options: Empathy
Mood
Competence
Altruism
questions.explanation: A good mood increases the likelihood of helping, so people who have just had a pleasant experience help more. Competence refers to having the skills to help, not to how a person feels.

questions.stem: Two passers-by see a person collapse. The one trained in first aid is more likely to step in. Which factor best explains this?
options: Competence
Mood
Reciprocity
Audience inhibition
questions.explanation: Feeling competent, or having the skills needed to help, makes people more confident to act and more likely to help. Audience inhibition would make a person less likely to act.

questions.stem: Altruism is:
options: helping others in order to receive something back in the future
helping only when other people are watching and will approve of it
helping because a person in authority has ordered it
helping others with no expectation of reward, even at a cost to oneself
questions.explanation: Altruism is helping purely out of concern for others, with no expectation of reward and sometimes at a personal cost. Helping in order to receive something back is not altruistic.

questions.stem: Which example best shows altruism rather than reciprocity?
options: A stranger swims out to rescue a struggling swimmer and leaves without giving her name
A worker covers a colleague's shift because the colleague covered hers last week
A student lends her notes to a classmate who promises to share his notes in return
A neighbour waters a friend's garden after the friend minded her dog
questions.explanation: The rescuer helps at a risk to herself and seeks nothing in return, not even recognition, which is altruism. The other examples involve returning or expecting a favour, which is reciprocity.

questions.stem: In which situation is a passer-by most likely to help someone who has collapsed?
options: She is running late, in a bad mood, and has no first aid training
She is with friends who laugh and say the person is probably fine
She is alone, the emergency is clear, and she is trained in first aid
She is in a large crowd, the situation is unclear, and others look calm
questions.explanation: Being the only witness avoids diffusion of responsibility, a clear emergency avoids misinterpretation, and first aid skills give competence. A crowd, ambiguity and calm bystanders all reduce helping.
